insider_note: Writing x as (x+1)−1 in the numerator is the one algebraic trick that makes this question fall into the eˣ[f+f′] family — without it, xeˣ/(x+1)² looks like nothing this chapter has seen yet.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Rewrite the numerator and identify f(x), f′(x)
steps.why: Writing x as (x+1)−1 splits the fraction into 1/(x+1) and −1/(x+1)², which are exactly f(x) and f′(x) for f(x)=1/(x+1) — the derivative of 1/(x+1) genuinely is −1/(x+1)².
common_mistakes: Trying integration by parts on xeˣ/(x+1)² directly instead of rewriting the numerator first.
Writing x = (x+1)+1 instead of (x+1)−1, which gives the wrong split.
steps.memory_tip: x = (x+1) − 1, always — add and subtract 1 to match the denominator's own linear factor.

steps.label: Apply the formula for the final answer
steps.why: With f(x)=1/(x+1) identified, the standard eˣ[f+f′] result gives eˣ/(x+1) directly.
common_mistakes: Writing eˣ/(x+1)² instead of eˣ/(x+1) — the answer keeps f(x), not the f′(x) piece.
steps.memory_tip: The answer is eˣ times f(x) = 1/(x+1), the term with the SMALLER power in the denominator.
